historical_timeline.summary: Born in Hortonville, Sullivan County, New York.
His father, a physician, died of pneumonia.
Entered medical school at Columbia; later transferred to New York University.
Surgeon on the North Greenland expedition.
Physician of the Belgian Antarctic Expedition; recommended fresh seal meat for scurvy.
Claimed the first ascent of Mount McKinley (Denali).
Claimed to have reached the North Pole; the claim was later declared not proven.
Convicted of mail fraud in Texas and sentenced to 14 years and 9 months.
Imprisoned at Leavenworth, where he worked in the prison hospital.
Critically ill of apoplexy; granted a full presidential pardon.
Died in New Rochelle, New York.

claims.statement: Frederick Albert Cook was born on June 10, 1865, in Hortonville, New York, the fifth of six children of Theodor and Magdalena Koch (later Cook).

His father, a physician, died of pneumonia when Frederick was five, leaving the family poor; he worked at odd jobs while at school, entered the College of Physicians and Surgeons at Columbia University in 1887, transferred to New York University, passed his medical examinations, and opened a medical office in Manhattan.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented medical training; anchors his modern history as a physician. The father's cause of death is recorded in the family history.

claims.statement: He served as surgeon, ethnologist and photographer on Robert Peary's North Greenland expedition of 1891 to 1892.

As physician of the Belgian Antarctic Expedition (1897 to 1899), whose ship Belgica wintered in the pack ice, he recognized the signs of scurvy in the men and recommended that they eat fresh seal meat. On this expedition he met Roald Amundsen, who remained his supporter through the later controversies.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented work as an expedition physician; no illness of his own is recorded.

claims.statement: He claimed to have reached the summit of Mount McKinley (Denali) on the morning of September 16, 1906, with one companion. The claim has been disputed ever since and is widely regarded as untrue.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Career context; the dispute is documented, not a judgment made by this record.

source_links.locator: biographical note: the claim has been disputed
a claim proved to be fraudulent

claims.statement: He claimed to have reached the North Pole on April 21, 1908, with two Inuit companions, Ahwelah and Etukishook, after which they wintered in a cave at Cape Sparbo on Devon Island before returning in 1909. A commission of the University of Copenhagen, given his surviving records, declared the claim not proven, and Robert Peary, who claimed the Pole for April 6, 1909, disputed it publicly.
He organized the Petroleum Producers' Association in Texas in 1922. In 1923 he was convicted of mail fraud, fined $12,000 and sentenced to 14 years and 9 months.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented conviction; anchors the modern re-entry episode.

source_links.locator: charged with fourteen counts; sentenced in 1923

claims.statement: The Columbia Encyclopedia states that he served five years (1925 to 1930) of the sentence.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Differs from his own reckoning of six years and three months, which includes county jail; both are recorded.

claims.statement: He called it 'the greatest tragedy of my life' to have been a federal prisoner for six years and three months: sixteen months in the county jail at Fort Worth, Texas, and four years and eleven months at Leavenworth.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of his imprisonment.

claims.statement: At Leavenworth he served as a physician in the prison hospital and edited the prison newspaper, the New Era.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented work in prison; anchors his modern history.

claims.statement: He was paroled from Leavenworth in March 1930, at 64. The parole required that he 'write and speak nothing but the truth', the government was to take the first $12,000 he earned toward his fine, and he met reporters wearing a faded old suit before leaving for Chicago.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Places the start of his life after prison; anchors the modern re-entry episode. Time gives his age as 65; he turned 65 in June 1930.

source_links.locator: paroled in 1930, having served one third of his term

claims.statement: After his release he worked on his memoirs and led a relatively quiet life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented in general terms only; his whereabouts and health from 1930 to 1940 were not verified in a fetched source.

claims.statement: In May 1940 he lay critically ill of apoplexy at Port Chester, New York; told on his sickbed that he had been granted a full presidential pardon restoring his civil rights, he answered 'Thanks - happy' and sank back into a coma.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the episode. Documented stroke a decade after the synthetic episode; the modern episode makes no prediction about it.

claims.statement: He died on August 5, 1940, in New Rochelle, New York; the Ohio State University exhibit gives the cause as a cerebral hemorrhage.

source_links.locator: died in New Rochelle, NY in 1940
death from a cerebral hemorrhage in 1940

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Re-entry primary care for a 65-year-old former physician and explorer establishing care four months after release from about six years in prison: medication reconciliation without records; high blood pressure at the first visit confirmed with home readings (stage 2 hypertension, two first-line drugs under the 1929 AHA/ACC guideline, target below 130/80); a right carotid bruit evaluated with duplex ultrasound, which finds an asymptomatic 50 to 69 percent internal carotid stenosis managed with best medical therapy (a statin, low-dose aspirin, blood pressure control and yearly surveillance) rather than revascularization, and stroke warning signs; a drug-induced gout flare on hydrochlorothiazide, treated with low-dose colchicine and followed by a switch to losartan under the 1924 ACR gout guideline; hepatitis C, latent tuberculosis, HIV and hepatitis B screening after incarceration (USPSTF and CDC); depression and shame screening; housing, income, benefits and reputation as health needs; and the Welcome to Medicare preventive examination with vaccinations. Built on the 1929 AHA/ACC hypertension guideline, the 1928 AHA/ASA primary stroke prevention guideline, the SVS 1925 and ESVS 1927 carotid guidelines, the 1922 AHA/ACC cholesterol guideline, the CMID hypertension, hyperlipidemia and stroke monographs, the 1924 ACR gout guideline, and the USPSTF and CDC recommendations.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Cook returns two weeks after his first visit, on the day of his carotid duplex ultrasound and his consultation with Dr. Abernathy-Mensah. He measured his blood pressure at home twice a day for seven days with the upper-arm cuff from the clinic; the fourteen readings average 154/90. He has had no headache, chest pain, breathlessness, weakness, numbness, speech trouble or loss of vision in either eye. He has cut down on salt and walks each day. He has signed the request for his prison medical records, which have not yet arrived, and has met the social worker once. He feels low at times and ashamed when people recognize his name, but he is sleeping and writing.

assessment_plan.assessment: The raised office readings at intake (166/94) are confirmed by home readings averaging 154/90, so this is stage 2 hypertension. Baseline tests are reassuring: sodium 140 and potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.98 mg/dL (eGFR 86), fasting glucose 94 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.5%, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 18 mg/g, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, and an ECG without left ventricular hypertrophy. For stage 2 hypertension the 1929 AHA/ACC guideline recommends starting two first-line drugs of different classes. With carotid atherosclerosis the target is below 130/80
plan: Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg each morning and amlodipine 5 mg daily
Sodium, potassium and creatinine in about four weeks

assessment_plan.assessment: The right carotid bruit heard at intake now has its explanation. Duplex today shows a 50 to 69 percent stenosis of the right internal carotid artery (peak systolic velocity 165 cm/s, end-diastolic velocity 38 cm/s, ratio 2.6) and less than 50 percent plaque on the left, with no symptoms of stroke or transient ischemic attack. Dr. Abernathy-Mensah recommends best medical therapy rather than endarterectomy or stenting, which are considered for asymptomatic stenosis of 70 percent or more. LDL cholesterol 148 mg/dL

assessment_plan.assessment: A typical first gout flare of the big toe (podagra), with sudden overnight onset, redness, swelling and maximal tenderness within a day, in a man taking a thiazide diuretic, which raises serum urate. No fever, no skin break, and a single typical joint make septic arthritis unlikely, so the joint was not aspirated; he will return at once if he develops fever or the joint worsens. Serum urate can be falsely normal during a flare, so it will be measured once the flare has settled. Low-dose colchicine is chosen: an oral NSAID would add to the bleeding risk of aspirin and raise blood pressure that is not yet at target. Atorvastatin with colchicine slightly raises the risk of muscle toxicity at higher colchicine doses; the short low-dose course is acceptable with a warning about muscle pain

assessment.assessment: Atherosclerotic, moderate and asymptomatic: he has had no stroke, transient ischemic attack or transient monocular blindness, and the examination is normal. The bruit led to the duplex, which is evaluation of a sign rather than population screening. The annual stroke risk with asymptomatic moderate stenosis on modern medical therapy is low, about 1 percent a year or less. Endarterectomy is considered for asymptomatic stenosis of 70 to 99 percent in suitable patients when the surgical stroke and death risk is below 3 percent, so revascularization is not indicated at 50 to 69 percent. Best medical therapy is the treatment. Brain imaging would not change management now
Confirmed by home readings. Lowering blood pressure is safe with a stenosis of this degree and is the most effective single measure against stroke; the target is below 130/80
